source.title: Interpretability as Compression: Reconsidering SAE Explanations of Neural Activations with MDL-SAEs
source.authors: K. Ayonrinde; Michael T. Pearce; Lee Sharkey

page_placements.theme: Feature granularity depends on the sparsity setting (L0/L1), not only width

record.tranche_reason: The paper gives a toy-model analysis of when sparsity favors feature splitting and when minimizing description length instead avoids it; this refines the proposed account of splitting, but does not train or evaluate larger language-model SAEs.
record.gate_note: The paper cites feature splitting in larger dictionaries from prior work; those cited results are not recorded as rows. Its MNIST SAE experiments concern feature appearance and description length, not splitting or relations between dictionary sizes, so they are not rows for these versions.
record.test_reason: Section 6 gives an analytic toy argument about objectives. On correlated Boolean inputs, the sparsity (L0) objective always prefers a split representation at equal reconstruction. An MDL objective avoids splitting unless the correlation is high. This is a specific argument bearing on V6. No trained-SAE splitting is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that minimising L0 always favours splitting correlated features even with no reconstruction gain. MDL gives a decision criterion, avoiding splitting at low correlation and allowing it when the conjunction is frequent. They also argue hierarchical (tree) SAE architectures would give shorter descriptions. The splitting analysis is a hypothesised mechanism shown in toy models, not measured in trained SAEs.
record.recipe_differences: An analytic Boolean toy-model comparison using L0 and description length; no experimental sweep of trained SAEs across dictionary sizes.
record.method_sensitivity: The MDL preference changes with the correlation between A and B.

fits_no_version.finding: MNIST BatchTopK SAEs at matched test MSE. Wide, low-L0 SAEs learn digit-template features; narrow, high-L0 SAEs learn point-like or dense features; the MDL optimum yields stroke-like features (Fig. 3).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Feature granularity changes with SAE width/L0 at fixed reconstruction, and description length selects an intermediate granularity.

record.problems: The splitting analysis is theoretical and limited to a Boolean toy model; it does not empirically establish the proposed mechanism in trained language-model SAEs. The MNIST experiments do not test splitting.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted under the 60-row limit.

untested.parts: No SAEs are trained at increasing dictionary sizes, and the geometric closeness of finer features to coarse ones is not measured. The only splitting result is a constructed toy.
No large models or open SAE releases are analysed for splitting. GPT-2 SAEs appear only in a description-length calculation.
No learned feature families or geometry are measured. Hierarchy is discussed only theoretically (Section 7).

No measurement of parent latents failing to fire. No tests of whether SAE size or sparsity changes fix it. Section 7 only argues that a sparse SAE would learn mutually exclusive 'Bird' and 'Generic Animal' features.
No comparison of latents across SAE sizes.

No trained SAE on correlated or hierarchical inputs is checked for splitting, and no alternative objective (MDL-SAE or Matryoshka) is trained to show reduced splitting. All evidence is analytic toy reasoning.

missing.what: Analytic argument that a sparsity-optimised SAE represents hierarchical concepts as mutually exclusive features ('Bird' vs 'Generic Animal' A∧¬B), never as parent plus child. A tree-structured code has lower description length but higher L0 (Fig. 5). This bears on the objective-artifact account and on absorption-like behaviour.

record.verdict_notes: Only the V6 verdicts are given, and all rest on analytic toy derivations, not trained-SAE measurements. The reader's V1 'supports' label is dropped because R1 is a construction, not a dictionary-size result. R3 is relabelled from limits_scope to supports, since an alternative objective reducing splitting is what V6 says. R4 alone limits scope. The V4-relevant hierarchy argument (Section 7) is listed as missing rather than given a verdict, because it neither measures firing nor tests size/sparsity changes.

versions.untested_parts: Only a constructed Boolean toy model is compared; the paper does not train SAEs at increasing dictionary sizes or measure geometric closeness of learned features.
No results on large models or open SAE releases.
No learned feature families or nested geometric hierarchy are measured.
No parent-child latent firing or interventions on SAE size or sparsity are tested.
No decomposition of larger SAE latents into smaller SAE latents or assessment of novel latents.
The analysis is a Boolean toy model, not a trained model or SAE experiment; hierarchical inputs are discussed theoretically, and Matryoshka SAEs are not tested.

rows.subject: toy model of undesirable feature splitting
rows.operation_detail: Compare two Boolean features with a representation using three mutually exclusive features, including an explicit A∧B feature.

conditions.value: Boolean A and B; four possible activation states

rows.measure: Reconstruction of the possible activation states
rows.baseline: Two Boolean features A and B; reconstructs A∧B as vA+vB
rows.value: Three mutually exclusive features for A∧¬B, B∧¬A, and A∧B; same reconstruction error
rows.note: A stylized construction, not a trained SAE size sweep. The paper does not quantify direction similarity.
rows.check: This is the stipulated setup of the toy construction (two candidate representations), not a result. The paper never grows a dictionary or measures directions, so it does not bear on V1. It should be merged into the description of R2–R4, not kept as a result row.

rows.subject: toy model of undesirable feature splitting
rows.operation_detail: Compare expected L0 for the unsplit and split Boolean representations.

conditions.value: pA and pB; split-state probabilities as defined in the text

rows.value: Split: pA + pB − pA∧B; the text states this is necessarily lower
rows.note: The text says the split representation has the same reconstruction error as the unsplit representation.
rows.check: Analytic derivation, not an experiment. The split representation has lower L0 (pA+pB−pA∧B) at the same reconstruction error, so the sparsity objective favours splitting on correlated inputs.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6, 'No Feature Splitting' / 'Feature Splitting' paragraphs and Fig. 4 caption

rows.subject: toy model of undesirable feature splitting
rows.operation_detail: Compare description length of split and unsplit representations.
rows.value: Unsplit representation takes fewer bits; feature splitting is not preferred by MDL
rows.note: The paper describes the result qualitatively; no numerical threshold for ρ is stated.
rows.check: Analytic phase diagram (Fig. 4C) with pA=pB. At small correlation ρ an MDL objective does not prefer splitting, so a different objective reduces it. No numeric threshold is given.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6, paragraph after the L0 derivation; Fig. 4C phase diagram (pA = pB)

rows.subject: toy model of undesirable feature splitting
rows.operation_detail: Compare description length of split and unsplit representations.
rows.value: Feature splitting is preferred by MDL because A∧B occurs frequently enough that explicit representation reduces description length
rows.note: The paper describes the result qualitatively; no numerical threshold for ρ is stated.
rows.check: Analytic. At large ρ, MDL also prefers splitting, so some splitting is justified by the data statistics rather than being a pure artifact of the sparsity objective. This bears on V6's 'says little about the model's units' part.

source_check.locator_found: Section 6, paragraph after the L0 derivation; Fig. 4C phase diagram (pA = pB)

relationships.condition: Analytic Boolean toy model; L0 sparsity objective vs MDL at low correlation
relationships.reason: Sparsity always prefers the split representation at equal reconstruction (R2). MDL avoids splitting when A and B are weakly correlated (R3). Section 7 also argues sparsity never favours hierarchical parent/child coding (text, not in rows).
relationships.display_finding: At equal reconstruction, the sparsity objective always preferred the split representation, while MDL avoided splitting when A and B were weakly correlated. The authors also argue that sparsity never favours hierarchical parent/child coding.

relation.reason: The study's own analytic toy results bear on whether V6 holds. It does not only cite or use the finding.

tranche.reason: Section 6 gives a specific analytic argument: the L0 objective always favours splitting, while MDL avoids it at low correlation and allows it at high correlation. This qualifies how V6 should be stated. It is not a same-method test.

source_check.notes: Analytic toy only (pA = pB, phase diagram Fig. 4C, no numeric ρ threshold), with no trained-SAE test of splitting. The authors call it a hypothesised mechanism. R4's 'observed' state means MDL prefers splitting at high ρ, which qualifies V6 (l1 limits_scope) rather than confirming it. The study shares authors with an original, so it is not an independent test.
